issues.issue: The extension operates only "to the extent such Collective Bargaining Agreement is not modified by, or inconsistent with," this Memorandum, which leaves the reach of the qualifier and which terms survive open to argument. "Inconsistent with" is not defined and would have to be applied clause by clause.

The Memorandum extends the CBA to March 30, 2000, but Appendix A.B(2) ties a guarantee to "the expiration date of the current Collective Bargaining Agreement," leaving it unclear whether that is 1993 or 2000. A court could be asked to reconcile the two.
A "restated commitment" to orderly start-up and to "negotiate those issues" is aspirational language of uncertain obligatory force. Whether it creates any enforceable duty is arguable.

This preambular commitment to negotiate issues at other new or rebuilt facilities sits against paragraph 1.C, which sends unresolved facility disputes to binding interest arbitration after 120 days. A court could be asked which controls.

The blanket application at "any new or rebuilt facility" is cut back by the May 16 side letter stating that all references to "new and rebuilt facilities" do not apply to 43rd Street or the staging facility. The interaction of the two is a possible construction point.

"e.g. palletization, tractor-trailer delivery to wholesalers, and card reader system" are illustrations of an open-ended category of innovations, practices and "working conditions," so the catch-all's reach is uncertain. A court could be asked whether unlisted changes qualify.

The 120-day period has no stated start date and "further technological innovations, methods of operation, scheduling practices, and/or working conditions" is an open category. Whether a given dispute is arbitrable under this clause would turn on those words.

The paragraph is headed "The Contract Arbitrator" but its text speaks only of the "Merits Arbitrator," and it separately mentions a Status Quo Arbitrator, so the identity of the arbitrator named is uncertain. The mismatch between caption and text is a nameable defect.

The clause selects a new Status Quo Arbitrator "pursuant to the procedure described in paragraph B above," but section 2 contains no lettered paragraph B. The broken cross-reference leaves the applicable selection procedure to be construed.

"Necessary manning reductions" and "the most fair and equitable manner" are undefined and set no measurable standard. The summary is also expressly subordinate to Attachments A and B, raising which text governs on a discrepancy.

This definition requires an individual to be on the Group I list at signing AND still on it at ratification, while Attachment B eligibility asks only whether the individual is on the list "effective the date of ratification." The two eligibility tests do not match.

"In lieu of and not in addition to those that would otherwise be called for by the Agreement" leaves unclear which otherwise-payable contributions are displaced by the 450-FTE minimum. That phrase is the kind of term a fund and an employer would read differently.

The 450-FTE floor is raised by the side letter on FTEs employed in excess of 370 and reduced by the 1996 Health and Welfare letter, so the operative minimum is the product of three documents. Reconciling them is a genuine construction question.
"Commencing promptly after ratification" fixes no date for the start of the 45-day window. The trigger for the several rights keyed to closure of the buyout period is therefore imprecise.

The obligation to add employees "necessary to reach 370 regular situations" drawn only from non-accepting Eligible Group I Employees may be unfulfillable, and paragraph 4.D contemplates attrition below 370 with no obligation to promote. The two paragraphs pull in different directions.

The floor of "no less than 270 RSHs during the term" is hard to square with paragraph 4.D, which lets The Times eliminate or consolidate vacated situations at its discretion as attrition below 370 occurs. Which provision limits the other is a real question.
"Specific manning requirements" is the operative exception but is nowhere defined in the Memorandum. Its content would have to be construed from the underlying contract or practice.

The clause gives The Times discretion to fill or eliminate vacated situations subject only to undefined "specific manning requirements," and "following discussion with the Union" imposes no ascertainable standard. Both phrases are open to competing readings.

Unfettered elimination of vacated situations is difficult to reconcile with paragraph 4.B's 270-RSH floor and the Appendix A employment guarantees. A court could be asked to imply limits so those provisions retain effect.

The clause speaks of reorganizing "all existing daily West Side Direct routes, including both daily and Sunday routes," which is self-contradictory, and applies a 50% reduction that then yields fixed numbers of routes and assignments. Whether the percentage or the stated numbers governs is arguable.

The reorganization is said to be "subject only to" the 40-route minimum, yet the Saturday Night Bulldog side letter imposes a further limitation that the forty existing finishing times remain unchanged. The word "only" conflicts with that letter.
A 4:00 p.m. starting-time cap must be squared with the side letter freezing the forty current SNBD finishing times for the contract's duration. Together they may over-constrain the schedule.
"An alternate billing system" and "recovery routes" are undefined, so the scope of the elimination of cash collections is uncertain. The carve-out for recovery routes has no stated boundary.

After enumerating strikes, job actions and acts honoring picket lines, the clause sweeps in "any other acts that interfere with the Publisher's operations," leaving the catch-all's reach against the specifics uncertain. Ejusdem generis would be the battleground.

Release turns on a determination of "no substantial compliance" by the issuing tribunal, an undefined standard, and the five working days and five day period are stated inconsistently. Both would have to be construed to apply the clause.

The reopener sends the wage dispute to "binding arbitration" without identifying the arbitrator or forum, while barring consideration of "wage givebacks below the then current scale." Both the forum and the scope limitation invite argument.

The sentence is mechanically broken — "reapportion the contributions due on those increases between its pension plan and its health and welfare plan the total pension (8%) and health and welfare (7.68%) plan contributions made by The Times" has words missing — so it is unclear whether reapportionment reaches only contributions due on the increases or the entire 15.68%. That is the core of any dispute over what the Union may elect.

Any reapportionment right must be read against paragraph 3.A(3), which fixes health and welfare contributions for 1992-1995 at a 450-FTE minimum and declares them "in lieu of and not in addition to" other contributions. Whether reapportionment can alter those fixed contributions is a genuine internal tension.

The listed COLA dates skip March 31, 1996 yet the proviso applies to "all such adjustments beginning on March 31, 1992," a date not in the list and before the Memorandum's wage schedule. The mismatch of dates is a nameable mechanical defect.

Eligibility here is keyed to RSHs "on The New York Times Steady Situation list," whereas paragraph 3.A offers the buyout to "all active NMDU RSHs employed by the Times, including foremen." The two descriptions of the eligible population may not be coextensive.
"Interest at prevailing market interest rates" fixes no index, date or method of calculation for the annuity purchase. The amount payable therefore depends on a term with no stated content.

The cross-reference incorporates paragraph 3-A(3), which is a general 450-FTE welfare minimum for 1992-1995 rather than a buyout-specific obligation, so what contributions are owed "on behalf of" buyout takers is unclear. Reading the two together is a real construction task.

The election form surrenders "his or her contractual guarantee of employment," a guarantee whose terms are set by Appendix A and limited to individuals listed on Attachments 1 and 2. Whether a buyout taker had such a guarantee to surrender depends on Appendix A.
